title: Teacher Workflow No. 13: they revised the commas
author: Doan Winkel
source: howtoteachwithai.substack.com (How to Teach With AI), October 19, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel's thirteenth Teacher Workflow tackles a familiar grading trap: a second draft that differs from the first only by a dozen fixed commas still earns a better grade, which teaches students that polish is revision. Because no teacher can hold two versions of thirty papers in mind, he proposes using a chat tool to compare the drafts side by side and classify every change as structure, evidence, polish or none. The five-step workflow, about two hours for a section of thirty, begins with scrubbing and coding student papers so no names or accommodation notes are pasted. It then runs one pair per chat with a fixed prompt, and requires the teacher to verify three pairs by hand before trusting the batch. Verified comparisons feed three-sentence revision feedback that the teacher edits, and a final class tally shows whether the teacher's own draft-one comments asked for structural change or only polish. A smallest version applies the first three steps to the five students whose second drafts look suspiciously clean.
points: Grading only the final product rewards polish, so the workflow has the AI report what changed between drafts and lets the teacher grade the revision itself.
Privacy comes first: students are replaced with codes, the key stays on the teacher's machine, and only a campus-approved tool is used.
A three-pair spot check, covering a structural case, a polish or none case and the longest list, decides whether the batch can be trusted or whether the teacher must read the drafts personally.
The tool compares and the teacher still grades, and every piece of feedback is edited with a line only the teacher could write.
Tallying change types against the teacher's own comments reveals whether students revised what the comments pointed at, which may mean fewer comma notes next round.
quotes: Draft two is on your desk. Same thesis, same paragraphs in the same order, a dozen commas fixed and a new title.
Week seven is when second drafts land, and you grade them the way you graded the first: read the final thing, score it.
A chat tool can. It reads both drafts side by side and reports what actually changed. You check its work, then grade the revision instead of the result.
Replace each student’s name with a code: S01, S02, S03, etc. Keep the key in a file on your own machine. It never gets pasted.
Open both drafts and confirm every quoted before-and-after line exists and says what the tool claims.
Edit every one before it goes back, and add the line only you could write. The tool did the comparing. You are still the grader.
Skip it and you keep handing out B+ grades for fixed commas, and your students keep believing that is what revision means.
